title: U of T Engineering to host new research chair in nuclear fusion energy
excerpt: Chair is part of the Centre for Fusion Energy, a national hub that bridges government labs, academic institutions and industry
content:
On November 13, government, industry and academia gathered at U of T Engineering to mark the launch of Canada’s newest research chair in fusion energy. 

Those in attendance included the Honourable Nolan Quinn, Ontario’s Minister of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security, MPP Rudy Cuzzetto, Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Energy and Mines, and MP Danielle Martin (University-Rosedale). 

They were joined by senior officials from Atomic Energy of Canada Limited (AECL), Canadian Nuclear Laboratories (CNL), Ontario Power Generation (OPG) and Stellarex. 

The new chair is the result of a request for information initiated through the Centre for Fusion Energy (CFE). Together, the partners have pledged $5 million for the new chair; the chairholder will be announced next year. 

“Recent research breakthroughs in Canada and around the world have brought the long-standing dream of fusion energy much closer to practical reality,” says Professor Stark Draper (ECE), Vice-Dean Research at U of T Engineering. 

“This new research chair will further accelerate that work. We are very proud to be selected as the host institution. Based at U of T, the new research chair will spark new collaborations and innovations among researchers whose expertise spans all aspects of nuclear technology — including physics, engineering, materials science, computational science and energy systems — helping to advance this globally important field.”  

Today, all commercial-scale nuclear plants operate via nuclear fission, a process by which large atoms such as uranium break apart into smaller ones, releasing heat energy as they do. 

Nuclear fusion is the opposite: it involves smashing isotopes of hydrogen — the lightest element — together until they fuse into helium. This process, similar to that which powers the sun, releases enormous amounts of energy that can be used to generate electricity. 

Whether it’s fission today or fusion in the future, nuclear power plays a critical role in the rising need for reliable sources of low-carbon electricity. 

Already, nuclear makes up nearly a third of Ontario’s generation capacity, and because it runs continuously as baseload power, accounts for between 40 and 50% of its generation. The shift to EVs and electrification across other sectors will raise demand significantly in the decades to come. 

The new chair will serve as a key component of the Centre for Fusion Energy, which is a national hub that bridges government labs, academic institutions and industry to accelerate fusion technology and build Canadian capabilities. 

“Building Canada’s nuclear future can only be done by working together and generating momentum with investments that move the field forward. The CFE enables interested partners across Canada to create new partnerships and fund strategic projects that solve common challenges,” says Dr. Amy Gottschling, AECL’s Vice-President of Science, Technology, and Commercialization. 

U of T is home to Canada’s top-ranked engineering school, and consistently ranks among the world’s leading research universities. It is home to initiatives such as the Atomic Energy Materials & Systems (AEMS) cluster founded by Professor Nazir Kherani (MSE, ECE). 

AEMS integrates multidisciplinary research, training and external partnerships in the nuclear space, with fusion as one of its key pillars. Kherani was among the key architects of a new MEng emphasis in Nuclear Engineering, which launched earlier this year. 

Over the summer, U of T joined CNL’s Academic Partnership Program, which will facilitate student research placements, specialized workshops and conferences and expanded collaboration between university and industry researchers. 

“Ontario and Canada are marking another major milestone in our plan to harness Ontario’s nuclear advantage and secure the clean, reliable energy needed to power our future,” says Nolan Quinn, Minister of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security. 

“University of Toronto is a proven research powerhouse, and as host to our new Centre for Fusion Energy Research Chair, the university will play a critical role in advancing clean energy innovation by driving transformative fusion research.” 

“OPG has a proud history of advancing nuclear innovation, and we see tremendous potential for fusion to help meet growing clean energy needs in Ontario and around the world,” says Kim Lauritsen, OPG’s Senior Vice President – Enterprise Strategy and Growth.

“This new research chair will help drive the scientific breakthroughs, expertise and collaboration needed to accelerate fusion technology and bring commercial applications closer to reality.”

“Fusion energy represents one of the most exciting scientific and technological opportunities of our time, with the potential to provide abundant, reliable and carbon-free energy for future generations,” says Dr. Monica Regalbuto, CNL’s Vice-President of Science and Technology. 

 “While much work remains to turn that promise into reality, Canada is well positioned to be a leader in the field. The Centre for Fusion Energy is helping to build the national ecosystem required to achieve that goal, and we are proud to support its continued growth through this investment in leadership, research and collaboration.”
